meta.title: Three information-technology transitions: movable-type printing, the World Wide Web, generative AI
meta.curator: CHRONOS development session 2026-10-17 (AI-assisted curation; requires review by a historian/economist)
meta.verification_policy: Every reference marked metadata_checked had its bibliographic data (authors, venue, year, and where stated the headline numbers) checked against at least one external index or the publisher page via web search on 2026-10-17. No reference is marked content_checked: no person has yet confirmed that each cited passage supports each claim. Evidence levels are curator assessments, not outputs of CHRONOS statistics.
known_gaps: No machine-readable diffusion series for printing is loaded (Buringh & van Zanden book-production estimates are published by OWID as a chart, but the chart API host was unreachable during development).
Generative-AI evidence covers 2022-2026 only: no long-run outcome can be observed yet.
Internet-user shares come from ITU press material; ITU revises its own estimates (2019: 54% first, later 51%).

references.title: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early-Modern Europe
references.notes: Title/year confirmed indirectly via reviews of Johns (1998) that discuss it.

references.title: The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making
references.notes: Some reviews cite a 2000 printing. Argues that 'Eisenstein's print culture does not exist' (p. 19); fixity and authority of print were achieved, not intrinsic.

references.title: Information Technology and Economic Change: The Impact of the Printing Press
references.notes: Cities that adopted printing 1450-1500 (about 200 of over 1,000 cities) grew about 60% faster 1500-1600 than similar cities; no prior growth advantage; distance from Mainz used as instrument.

references.venue: CEP Discussion Paper 1600, London School of Economics
references.notes: Printing output and competition in European cities 1454-1600; printer deaths as exogenous variation; business-education and Reformation content. Journal publication not confirmed.

references.title: Printing and Protestants: An Empirical Test of the Role of Printing in the Reformation
references.notes: Bibliographic data confirmed; the headline estimate was not retrieved in this session.

references.notes: Book production grew about 1%/yr on average over the long run; the post-1450 rise attributed mainly to lower book prices and higher literacy; authors call their figures low estimates.

references.title: Incunabula Short Title Catalogue (ISTC)

references.title: General purpose technologies 'Engines of growth'?

references.venue: American Economic Review: Papers and Proceedings 80(2): 355-361

references.authors: Eloundou, Tyna; Manning, Sam; Mishkin, Pamela; Rock, Daniel

mechanisms.name: Falling marginal cost of reproducing and distributing information
mechanisms.description: A technology cuts the cost of copying (printing), distributing (web) or producing (generative AI) text and code, expanding supply and access.

mechanisms.name: Complementary intangible investment delays measured productivity gains (J-curve)
mechanisms.description: Gains from a general-purpose technology require reorganisation, skills and intangible capital; measured productivity can stagnate or fall before rising.

mechanisms.name: Task displacement and reinstatement
mechanisms.description: Technology substitutes for some tasks and complements others, reallocating labour across tasks and occupations; wages follow the balance of the two.

mechanisms.name: Uneven gains across skill levels
mechanisms.description: Gains concentrate on less experienced workers (compression) or on skilled complements (skill bias), changing inequality.

mechanisms.name: Growth advantage of early-adopting places and firms
mechanisms.description: Places and firms that adopt early gain market access, human capital and business knowledge; advantages can persist.

mechanisms.name: Contestation of established authorities and of information quality
mechanisms.description: Cheaper dissemination lets new ideas (and misinformation) bypass gatekeepers, challenging religious, political or scientific authority.

mechanisms.name: Institutional and regulatory response with a lag
mechanisms.description: Rules, rights and censorship regimes adjust to the technology years after diffusion begins.

mechanisms.name: General-purpose technology dynamics
mechanisms.description: Pervasive use, continuing improvement and innovational complementarities (Bresnahan & Trajtenberg).

claims.statement: Printing lowered the cost of books, which together with rising literacy drove the post-1450 surge in book production.

references.locator: abstract: rise attributed to lower prices and literacy
print's authority and fixity were constructed, not automatic

alternatives.description: Rising literacy and urban demand (universities, laity) may have driven demand independently of the cost fall; the two are hard to separate.

claims.statement: Early adoption of printing caused faster city growth 1500-1600 (about 60% faster than similar cities).

references.locator: IV estimates using distance from Mainz

alternatives.description: Printers may have chosen already-promising locations (selection); Dittmar reports no prior growth advantage and instruments adoption with distance from Mainz.
The instrument would be invalid if distance from Mainz affected growth through other channels (e.g. trade networks along the Rhine).

claims.statement: Access to printing raised the likelihood that cities adopted Protestantism.

references.locator: competition among printers and Reformation content

alternatives.description: Political economy of rulers and cities (fiscal and power motives) as primary drivers; printing as an amplifier rather than a cause.

claims.statement: Print created a new 'print culture' (standardisation, fixity, preservation) that transformed early-modern knowledge.

references.locator: p. 19: 'Eisenstein's print culture does not exist'

alternatives.description: Fixity and credibility of print were achieved through social conventions and institutions, not by the technology itself.

claims.statement: The slow productivity payoff of computers parallels electrification: gains required reorganisation and arrived with a long lag.

references.locator: IT's effects smaller than earlier great inventions

claims.statement: After a lag, IT investment and IT-producing industries drove the US productivity acceleration of the mid-1990s.

alternatives.description: Much of the acceleration came from productivity in IT-producing sectors (semiconductors) rather than from internet use in the wider economy.
Cyclical factors and measurement (unmeasured intangibles) can shift the apparent timing of gains.

claims.statement: Computerisation substituted for routine tasks and complemented non-routine analytic and interactive work.

alternatives.description: Trade and offshoring also reduced demand for routine tasks over the same period.

claims.statement: CERN released the WWW code into the public domain so that the web could act as an open standard.
An open, royalty-free web standard contributed to internet diffusion reaching about half of humanity by 2019.

alternatives.description: Mobile phones, falling hardware prices and telecom liberalisation were probably larger drivers of the 2000s-2010s diffusion than the web's licensing.

claims.statement: Both printing and the web sharply lowered the cost of distributing text; this is an analogy, not a causal link.
The Transformer architecture is the technical basis of the GPT models behind ChatGPT.

alternatives.description: Compute scaling, data and reinforcement learning from human feedback were equally necessary conditions.

claims.statement: Generative AI raises productivity on specific tasks (writing, customer support, coding), with larger gains for less experienced workers.

references.locator: average time savings about 3% in the Danish survey (earlier version)

alternatives.description: External validity: short, self-contained experimental tasks may overstate gains in real jobs; output accuracy was not always verified.

claims.statement: Two years after adoption, generative AI has not measurably changed earnings or hours in exposed occupations.

references.locator: modest macro TFP effect (<=0.66% over 10 years)
J-curve: early measured effects understate later gains

alternatives.description: Too early: complementary investment (J-curve) and reorganisation can delay effects, as with electricity and computers.
Denmark's institutions (wage setting, firm structure) may limit pass-through to earnings; results may not transfer to other labour markets.

claims.notes: No mechanism asserted: the evidence shows small effects so far, not why. The J-curve is one candidate explanation (see alternatives and c_ict_genai_analogy).

claims.statement: The spread of generative AI shaped the EU AI Act's rules on general-purpose AI models.

alternatives.description: The legislative process started before ChatGPT (Commission proposal of 2021), so the Act as a whole was not caused by generative AI; only parts may have been reshaped.

claims.statement: Small measured effects of generative AI so far resemble the early computer productivity paradox; whether a later payoff follows is unknown.
Generative AI lowers the time cost of producing text and code on well-defined tasks (production, not only distribution, of information becomes cheaper).

references.locator: about 3% average time savings in real jobs (earlier version)

alternatives.description: Time saved on drafting may be offset by checking, correcting and new tasks created by the tool (real-job time savings appear much smaller than in experiments).

outlook_hypotheses.statement: By 2035, a majority of employed adults in high-income countries use generative AI at work at least weekly.
outlook_hypotheses.falsified_if: Representative surveys (e.g. the Real-Time Population Survey used by Bick, Blandin & Deming) show weekly work use below 50% of employed adults in the US or EU in 2035.
outlook_hypotheses.notes: Grounded in the fastest documented adoption so far (39% of US adults had tried it by Aug 2024) and in the wide diffusion of earlier information technologies; trying a tool is not routine use.

outlook_hypotheses.statement: Task-level gains do not translate into a large acceleration of world GDP-per-person growth before the early 2030s.
outlook_hypotheses.falsified_if: World GDP per person grows at 3.0%/yr or more on average over 2026-2031 (Maddison/OWID data).
outlook_hypotheses.notes: Electrification and computers paid off with lags of decades; the analogy to generative AI is itself only level 2.

outlook_hypotheses.statement: Through 2035, labour-market effects of generative AI show up mainly as task reallocation within occupations, not as large aggregate falls in employment or hours.
outlook_hypotheses.falsified_if: Administrative data show average falls in hours or earnings above 5% in the most exposed occupations relative to less exposed ones by 2032.
outlook_hypotheses.notes: Not yet operationalised in CHRONOS: needs occupation-level labour data (no connector).

outlook_hypotheses.statement: Places and firms that adopt AI early gain a growth advantage over comparable late adopters, as early-printing cities did after 1500.
outlook_hypotheses.falsified_if: Credible designs (instrumented adoption or staggered roll-outs) find no productivity or growth difference between early and late adopting regions/firms by 2035.
outlook_hypotheses.notes: Transfer from 16th-century cities to 21st-century firms is a strong assumption; scale and market structure differ.

outlook_hypotheses.statement: Disputes over the authority and provenance of information intensify, and regulation keeps lagging deployment by several years.
outlook_hypotheses.falsified_if: NOT YET OPERATIONALISED: requires an agreed indicator of information-authority conflict; as stated the hypothesis is too vague to be falsified.
outlook_hypotheses.notes: Kept to show a commonly made argument that CHRONOS cannot test in its current form.
